sections.title: Continuous and simple
sections.content:
When we focus on an activity itself, starting before and continuing up to (and possibly beyond) a particular point of time, rather than focusing on actions as completed events, we use continuous forms:
• Ingrid can't come to the phone. She's washing her hair.
• As you're not using your car at the moment, can I borrow it?
• This time yesterday, I was flying over the Pacific.
• Was she wearing that red dress when you saw her?
We use simple forms to talk about general situations, habits, and things that are or were always true. We use the past simple for completed events:
• When I worked as a postman I got up at three o'clock every morning.
• Miguel doesn't play golf very well.
• These birds build their nests on the ground.
• The earthquake struck the area at midday yesterday. (past simple for completed events)
We also use simple forms with state verbs:
• She intends to work hard at school and go on to university.
• Did you understand the instructions we were given?
However, we can use continuous forms with these verbs when they describe something happening or changing:
• She was intending to talk to Tony about the idea, but she didn't get the opportunity.
• I'm understanding physics much better now that Mr Davies is teaching us.

sections.title: Perfect
sections.content:
We use perfect verb forms to describe one event or state from the point of view of a later time. The present perfect suggests a connection between something that happened in the past and the present time. Note, however, that the situation or event does not have to continue until the time of speaking, only to have some connection or relevance to the present time:
• I've finished that book you wanted, so you can borrow it now.
• Have you turned the heating off? I don't like it to be on when I'm not at home.
• Your nose is bleeding. Has somebody hit you?
The past perfect is used to locate a past event before another past event:
• I invited him out to dinner, but he said he had already eaten.
• By the time I picked up the phone, they had rung off.

sections.title: Combinations of perfect and continuous
sections.content:
We combine the perfect and continuous forms in the present perfect continuous to describe an activity in progress either at or recently before the time of speaking, and possibly beyond it:
• I have been following the discussions on the forum with great interest.
We can also use the present perfect continuous to talk about activities that have recently finished with some result that can be seen, heard, etc.:
• Look at the dirt on your clothes! Have you been digging in the garden again?
The past perfect continuous has a similar meaning. However, the point of reference is not 'now' (as it is with the present perfect continuous) but a point in the past:
• When we met Lena and Marko, they had been riding.
• It had been snowing heavily for hours and when I went to the door I couldn't open it.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: I ___ (write) this blog in a hotel room in Perth.
exercises.hint: Activity in progress at the time of speaking = present continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am writing
The present continuous describes a temporary action or situation in progress around the present moment. The key signals here are words like at the moment, today, currently, or right now. Compare with the present simple, which describes permanent facts or habitual actions.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: I ___ here a couple of hours ago.
exercises.hint: Specific past time with 'ago' = past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: arrived
Specific past time with 'ago' = past simple. The past simple requires a specific completed time; present perfect is used when the time is unspecified or the result matters now.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: I ___ pretty tired so this will only be a short post.
exercises.hint: Temporary state at the moment of speaking = present continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am feeling
The present continuous describes a temporary action or situation in progress around the present moment. The key signals here are words like at the moment, today, currently, or right now. Compare with the present simple, which describes permanent facts or habitual actions.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: before I ___ to sleep.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: go
After conjunctions like 'before', 'when', 'until', and 'as soon as', use the present simple to refer to the future. English does not use 'will' in these subordinate time clauses.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: As you ___ , I spent last week in Adelaide with Ruby.
exercises.hint: State verb 'know' used in present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: know
State verb 'know' used in present simple. State verbs describe mental states, emotions, or senses and are not normally used in continuous forms.

exercises.question: He ___ (work) for the same company for 20 years and has no plans to leave.
exercises.hint: Still ongoing employment (from past to present) → present perfect (continuous).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: has been working / has worked
Both are possible, but the continuous emphasises the unbroken duration. Either expresses that the employment started in the past and continues now.

exercises.question: Amy's blog: I ___ (meet) her a month or so ago.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: met
The past simple is used for a specific completed action at a known or implied past moment. Here the action is finished and the time context is clear from the surrounding narrative.

exercises.question: Newspaper article: Aston United ___ their manager, Neil Ronson.
exercises.hint: Recent completed action with present relevance = present perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have sacked
Recent completed action with present relevance = present perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Newspaper article: The former England football international ___ (say) that he ___ the news when…
exercises.hint: Completed past events in sequence = past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: said / heard
Completed past events in sequence = past simple.

exercises.question: Newspaper article: he ___ from a three-week holiday in Spain.
exercises.hint: Event before another past event = past perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: had returned
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 Event before another past event = past perfect.

exercises.question: Newspaper article: 'There ___ no hint of any problem when I ___ (leave) for the holiday.'
exercises.hint: State before a past reference = past perfect; completed departure = past simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: had been / left
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 State before a past reference = past perfect; completed departure = past simple.

exercises.question: I ___ (just / realise) I left my keys at home.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have just realised
'Just' signals a very recent action with current relevance. This is a classic present perfect signal — the realisation has just happened and affects the present moment.

exercises.question: Conversation: Did he ___ any health problems recently?
exercises.hint: In a question about the period before now = present perfect simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have
In a question about the period before now = present perfect simple. The present perfect connects past events to the present moment — used for recent events, life experience, or ongoing results.

exercises.question: Conversation: well, he ___ from stress for some time.
exercises.hint: Ongoing situation up to now = present perfect continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: 's been suffering
Ongoing situation up to now = present perfect continuous. The present perfect connects past events to the present moment — used for recent events, life experience, or ongoing results.

exercises.question: Conversation: He ___ too hard for months.
exercises.hint: Activity lasting up to a reference point = past perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: had worked
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 Activity lasting up to a reference point = past perfect.

exercises.question: Conversation: ___ you gone up to Scotland when you ___ ?
exercises.hint: Present perfect for unspecified past up to now; past simple for specific event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Have / heard
Present perfect for unspecified past up to now; past simple for specific event. The past simple requires a specific completed time; present perfect is used when the time is unspecified or the result matters now.

exercises.question: Conversation: the doctors ___ him over.
exercises.hint: Completed action with present relevance = present perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have checked
Completed action with present relevance = present perfect. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: Conversation: and ___ (tell) him that he needs complete rest.
exercises.hint: Event before another past event = past perfect.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: had told
Event before another past event = past perfect.
